📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence. We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning latest ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote manufacturer. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

It has been revealed that are you passionate about data analytics and eager to work on large-scale projects? Fingerprint is looking for a Data Analyst to join our Identification Accuracy Team. You will be the team's go-to analyst for questions about how accurately we identify browsers and devices: investigating accuracy questions from Customer Success and Sales, building the reporting and dashboards those teams rely on, and turning repeat requests into self-service tools. Our Identification API Product processes approximately 1 billion requests per month, so you will work hands-on with large-scale event data and the models behind it.

Recent findings suggest that at Fingerprint, we believe in pay transparency — it's part of how we operate as a distributed, remote-first team. Salaries are based on function, level, and geographic location, benchmarked against similar stage growth companies.

Because this role is open across the United States and can be based anywhere our team members work from, the salary range reflects that geographic breadth: $115k - $155k.

Some example salaries for specific locations are below:.

Final offer amounts are determined by multiple factors, including the successful candidate's location, experience, and expertise, and may vary from the amounts listed above.

Industry observers note that due to regulatory and security reasons, there’s a small number of countries where we cannot have Fingerprint teammates based. Additionally, because Fingerprint is an all-remote firm and people can join our workforce from almost any country, we do not sponsor visas. Fingerprint teammates need to be authorized to work from their home location.

We are dedicated to creating an inclusive work environment for everyone. We embrace and celebrate the unique experiences, perspectives and cultural backgrounds that each employee brings to our workplace. Fingerprint strives to foster an environment where our employees feel respected, valued and empowered, and our team members are at the forefront in helping us promote and sustain an inclusive workplace. We highly encourage people from underrepresented groups in tech to apply.

If you are applying as a resident of California, please read our CCPA notice here.

If you are applying as a resident of the EU, please read our GDPR notice here.

In a recent development, **We have noticed a rise in recruiting impersonations across the industry, where scammers attempt to access candidates' personal and financial information through fake interviews and offers. All Fingerprint recruiting email communications will always come from the @fingerprint.com domain. Any outreach claiming to be from Fingerprint via other sources should be ignored.

    You dream of a fresh challenge, of being able to make a firm scale and feel that you have a real impact.

    If you dream of a life that is more like an adventure than a stable life, then becoming the AI-native right hand of our CEO is for you.

    This isn’t another chief of staff or right hand job.

    Most companies call themselves AI-first because they gave everyone a ChatGPT licence. We think that’s level 2, and there are 10.

    According to recent reports, at Paradox our ambition is $10M in revenue with 10 people, each of them running a dozen agents. Here, AI doesn’t assist the work. It runs the loops, in every department. Your job is to make that true for the whole manufacturer, side by side with the CEO.

    Deep inside you are looking for a upcoming adventure with….

    🗽Freedom: working remotely or hybrid, and being trusted to deliver.

    🔥Ambition: building one of the first truly AI-native companies, with teammates who push AI to its limits every week.

    😍Impact: changing the trajectory of a whole company, not one line of a roadmap, with a product that transforms people’s lives at scale.

    Then, you have found the next adventure that will fulfill you.

    In a organization of fewer than 10 people, the right hand used to be the person who absorbed everything the CEO couldn’t do. Here, the right hand builds the machine that does it.

    It has been revealed that hold the full context of Paradox. Our DNA, offers, decisions, procedures, member stories and past experiments, in one shared organization brain that every person and every agent reads before acting.

    Industry observers note that turn every decision into execution. A meeting, a voice note or a call with the CEO becomes briefs, tickets, follow-ups and deadlines, without anyone retyping it.

    Act across every tool. Not a chatbot in a tab: agents read and write in our whole stack, from code to CRM, billing, analytics, ads, email, calendar and documents.

    Sources indicate that ship. Produce the analysis, the contract draft, the page, the offer or the process, and put it live.

    According to recent reports, measure with real KPIs. Revenue, cash, margin, retention and the transformation of our members, not activity.

    Recent findings suggest that learn and loop on its own. Keep what works, kill what doesn’t, write the lesson back into the brain, and start the next cycle without waiting for a meeting.

    People set the ambition, the taste and the standards. The machine runs the loop, and gets better every week.

    This is already real. Our company brain holds our decisions and procedures. Our growth hub tracks every hypothesis and experiment with its result. Agents cut ads from long-form content, prepare webinars and audit our tracking after every live. And our product is AI-native too: Athena, our AI coach, works with members every day, by text and by voice.

    It has been revealed that we believe self-help is broken. Most people use learning platforms the same way: generic theory, a quick high, no real change.

    Research: Lack of Specialized Infrastructure Is a Top AI Adoption Challenge

    📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research Digital Realty.
    • It has been revealed that the Global Data Insights Survey 2026 points to a widening mix of infrastructure models behind enterprise AI.
    • Industry observers note that the research is based on an online survey of 2,131 IT decision-makers across 19 countries, and 11 industries, conducted from Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research Digital Realty. Forty percent of survey respondents cited a lack of specialized infrastructure required by AI as a main challenge to adopting a formal AI strategy, up from 9% in the firm's 2024 research.

    It has been revealed that the Global Data Insights Survey 2026 points to a widening mix of infrastructure models behind enterprise AI. Half of respondents host AI models in private clouds, 86% are pursuing or exploring sovereign AI, 92% tie data-location strategy to their AI looks, and 88% follow a distributed-data approach.

    Industry observers note that the research is based on an online survey of 2,131 IT decision-makers across 19 countries, and 11 industries, conducted from Nov. 23, 2025, through Feb. 4, 2026.

    Organizations also appear to be shifting from AI planning toward execution. The share actively executing AI to achieve operational efficiency or reduce costs rose from 27% in 2024 to 37% this year. Only 3% reported no measurable ROI to date, while 63% expect returns within the next six months to two years.

    Specialized infrastructure led the survey's list of AI adoption challenges at 40%, followed by regulatory and personal-data concerns at 35%. Data availability and quality, storage capacity, interconnection, compute resources, and staffing also ranked as significant constraints.

    According to recent reports, those requirements are also shaping workload placement. Integration with existing IT or data infrastructure ranked first at 43%, while regulatory compliance and performance were each cited by 37%. Data proximity, sovereignty, sustainability, cost, and intellectual property protection also factored into hosting decisions.

    Recent findings suggest that private cloud features prominently across the report's AI hosting categories, but enterprises are clearly using a mix of private cloud, public cloud, on-premises infrastructure, and colocation. Private cloud accounted for 50% of custom-built AI model hosting and 47% for open source or fine-tuned large language models (LLMs).

    It has been revealed that sovereignty is another part of that placement decision. Thirty-two percent consider sovereign AI — in which data and AI models remain within a single national or regulatory jurisdiction — a requirement, while another 54% are exploring it. The findings point toward hybrid environments in which infrastructure location, governance and data control increasingly overlap.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • Industry observers note that we’re looking for a Software Engineer to join Supabase’s Interfaces group and help run the backend services behind our developer tools, starting with postgres-meta: the open-source service that runs SQL against customers’ Postgres databases on behalf of our dashboard, our MCP server, AI agents, and other platform tools.
    • Industry observers note that AI agents are the fastest-growing source of postgres-meta’s traffic, and it sits on the path between developers and their data, so when it struggles, people can’t reach their databases from the dashboard or their agents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    Industry observers note that we’re looking for a Software Engineer to join Supabase’s Interfaces group and help run the backend services behind our developer tools, starting with postgres-meta: the open-source service that runs SQL against customers’ Postgres databases on behalf of our dashboard, our MCP server, AI agents, and other platform tools. You’ll work closely with the engineers who build those tools, and with our Platform and SRE teams.

    Industry observers note that AI agents are the fastest-growing source of postgres-meta’s traffic, and it sits on the path between developers and their data, so when it struggles, people can’t reach their databases from the dashboard or their agents. The team’s first priority is making it reliable, observable, and fair between tenants at agent scale, and helping redesign it for that scale without breaking the tools that depend on it. Depending on your experience, you’ll own major parts of that work or lead it. Alongside it, the team builds the backend services that give every branch of a project the configuration and secrets it needs.

    Industry observers note that we want to be upfront: this role carries real operational load. Our on-call process and rotation are new and need a lot of maturing, and you’ll help build them into something sustainable from your first weeks. You’ll be on call for services on the critical path, and incidents come before planned work. Platform teams run the infrastructure underneath; you’ll own the services themselves, from their code to how they behave in production. It’s ideal for someone who enjoys that kind of ownership, thrives in async, fast-paced environments, and stays calm when the root cause turns out to be in someone else’s system.

    It has been revealed that help mature the team’s on-call from your first weeks: grow the rotation to cover every service the team runs, write runbooks, and agree when to declare an incident. Then build it, with our embedded SRE, into a sustainable follow-the-sun rotation as the team grows.

    Set SLOs with the teams that call the service, and build the observability to hold them: metrics per tenant and per caller, alerts that catch failures wherever they start, and logs you can search across regions.

    Make deploys routine with canary and staged rollouts, so dependency and security upgrades stop being risky.

    Redesign how the service works with Postgres at scale: reusing connections, limiting or streaming large results, and isolating and rate-limiting tenants, so no single caller, human or agent, can degrade it for everyone else.

    Help decide the service’s long-term architecture with our Platform teams, then evolve it without breaking the callers that depend on it.

    Write down and agree the service’s contract with its callers, including the dashboard, MCP and AI, and platform workers: how transactions, multi-statement queries, timeouts, and errors behave.

    Work through incidents with the networking, Kubernetes, pooler, and control-plane teams when a problem on the path to customers’ databases starts in their systems.

    Build backend services for code-first workflows, starting with delivering each branch’s configuration and secrets to the services that need them.

    Make small changes directly in the CLI, dashboard, or docs when a capability needs them, with the owning team reviewing.

    Review code and designs, mentor other engineers, and grow into leading the team’s technical direction.

    Have 5+ years of experience as a software engineer, most of it building and running backend services in production.

    Have run a high-traffic, multi-tenant service in production: been on call for it, worked incidents through to resolution, and followed through on postmortems.

    Write strong TypeScript, and work confidently in a large Node.js backend codebase.

    Understand Postgres from the client side: connection management and pooling, transactions, statement timeouts and cancellation, and large result sets.

    Have built observability for a service you owned (metrics, tracing, logs, and alerts tied to SLOs), and used it to debug problems that span proxies, load balancers, or Kubernetes.

    Have kept a service healthy under load with patterns such as rate limiting, timeouts, memory limits, and graceful degradation.

    Have shipped changes to a live service safely, with canaries, staged rollouts, feature flags, or fast rollback.

    Work calmly and constructively with other teams during incidents, including when the root cause is in a system you don’t own.

    Communicate clearly in writing, from design docs to postmortems, thrive in async, globally distributed teams, and make progress when the path isn’t fully defined.

    Nice to have, roughly in order of how much they’d help:.

    Have rebuilt or migrated a live, high-traffic service without breaking its callers, using techniques such as shadow traffic, contract tests, or incremental replacement.

    Have led the design of reliability work, such as tenant isolation, load shedding, or a staged-deploy pipeline, or set technical direction that other engineers built on.

    Have built or operated a database proxy or connection pooler (such as PgBouncer, Supavisor, or pgcat), or an API gateway such as Envoy.

    Have secured a service that runs SQL on its callers’ behalf: handling credentials safely, and limiting how much damage any one caller can do.

    Production experience in a second backend language, such as Elixir or Go.

    Experience with a secrets manager or key management service, such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS KMS.

    Familiarity with Supabase, or with how AI agents use databases through tools like MCP.

    Industry observers note that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    • At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government.
    • Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured American to get life-changing aid.
    • Industry observers note that so far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured American to get life-changing aid. Our mission is to tear down barriers between people in crisis and the aid they deserve. In the last six years, we’ve become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We also help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    Industry observers note that so far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews. And we’re just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, Google Ventures, and True Ventures, and we’re on our way to creating a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    Recent findings suggest that in the next two years, we aim to help over 250,000 Americans get access to life-changing benefits. Much of that help reaches people through our Lawyer Network: our network of vetted partner law firms that represent clients alongside Atticus. The Lawyer Network (LN) team, led by Erin Casale, is the bridge between Atticus and those firms, and our job is to improve their ability to serve clients and help them grow.

    Sources indicate that we're hiring a Senior Account Manager to own our largest partner firms. You'll carry a deliberately small book of high-volume firms (roughly 10) and act as an extension of their team: diagnosing where and why they lose cases, coaching them on operations and legal execution, and getting even the most technophobic firm to adopt new Atticus tools.

    The ideal candidate has spent years making small business customers measurably better at what they do through a mix of operations and tech, and wants to do that work somewhere it changes lives.

    Make firms better. Own our enterprise-tier partner firms and improve their capacity, conversion rates, and win rates. Find best practices in firm operations and Social Security Disability legal execution, spread them across the network, and coach them relentlessly.

    Drive technology adoption. Get every firm, including folks who are tech-hesitant, using newly introduced Atticus features well. That means making the case for the value (think: sales motion but the product is free), building and implementing change management plans, and running training and support.

    Sources indicate that know your firms from the inside. Build relationships beyond the managing attorney, down to intake, case development, and operations leads. Understand a firm well enough to help with hiring, software, and staffing decisions, not just Atticus problems.

    Be the voice of firms inside Atticus. Bring what you learn back to Product, Customer Experience, and Operations so we serve firms better and learn from their experience.

    Deliver hard news well. Hold firms to clear performance standards and push back on attorneys—even those with decades of experience in the field—with finesse and confidence. If needed, cut ties gracefully.

    It has been revealed that shape how the team works. Own strategic projects end to end, from scoping the question and gathering data to sharing recommendations with leadership and rolling out what works across the network.

    5+ years in Account Management, Customer Success, Partnerships, or a similar role serving small businesses, where your mandate was improving your accounts' performance (not just retention).

    A track record of driving product adoption in a tech or tech-adjacent setting.

    You read data comfortably, spot trends before results move, and show up with both a diagnosis and a blueprint.

    You're persuasive in conversation and in writing, and you'd rather pick up the phone (or get on a plane) than send another email.

    You're outgoing and build trust quickly, with colleagues and with skeptical partners alike.

    Adaptable: resourceful and steady when priorities shift.

    You pick up new tools fast, from cloud software to building a clean deck.

    Recent findings suggest that we covered above why this job might be for you, and think it’s equally key to tell you why it might not be for you. You won’t enjoy this job very much if:.

    You prefer a large book of light-touch accounts over depth with a few.

    You want a predictable playbook.

    You get frustrated when projects and priorities change rapidly (we obviously try to limit this, but are a quickly-growing company and it does still happen).

    The role is a rare opportunity to join a fast-growing Series C startup that doubles as a B-corp social enterprise. Our team is still small enough for you to have an outsized impact on how we operate and how our firms grow.

    We offer competitive pay, including equity, and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employee and family premiums covered.

    15 vacation days and ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at end-of-year).

    $1,000 reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    We anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $110,000 and $130,000, in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as the candidate's experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    According to recent reports, this job is fully remote and we're committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the company dime) as needed to be with your colleagues, usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather. You'll also visit partner firms in-person occasionally. Overall, expect to travel up to monthly between internal get togethers and firm visits.

    Latest Update: OpenAI Intros Dots, AI Agents that Continue Working Between User Conversations

    📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OpenAI has introduced Dots, GPT-6 Astra-powered agents that run on their own cloud computers, using connected applications to carry on with assignments between conversations and incorporating people' feedback as they go.
    • Sources indicate that openAI is also previewing specialist Dots for organizations, with separate identities and credentials for defined responsibilities.
    • Industry observers note that the broader ambition seems to be to make delegation last beyond a chat session.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OpenAI has introduced Dots, GPT-6 Astra-powered agents that run on their own cloud computers, using connected applications to carry on with assignments between conversations and incorporating people' feedback as they go.

    Sources indicate that openAI is also previewing specialist Dots for organizations, with separate identities and credentials for defined responsibilities. Those enterprise deployments are beginning with focused pilots. The firm is working with Microsoft on integration with Agent 365's governance and security controls.

    Industry observers note that the broader ambition seems to be to make delegation last beyond a chat session. That change could reduce the need to repeatedly explain a project. It also makes supervision a continuing obligation: An instruction that was appropriate yesterday may no longer fit today's circumstances.

    One notable distinction appears in OpenAI's privacy and safety FAQ. Disconnecting an application stops upcoming access through that connection, but does not delete information already incorporated into a Dot's context.

    Users right now cannot inspect or directly edit individual Dot memories. Deleting a Dot deletes its own context, while files and conversations it created remain separately stored. Plugin permissions are shared across Dots, ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex.

    Recent findings suggest that for an organization, that creates two related governance questions: what an agent can retrieve now, and what it already knows. Revoking a connection addresses the first without necessarily resolving the second.

    Recent findings suggest that openAI's safety account distinguishes authorized tasks that continue in the background from unsolicited "proactive research." The latter uses tools restricted to reading permitted sources. Those research tasks cannot directly send messages, change connected application content, or control a browser or desktop. Any subsequent action must pass the usual rules and checks.

    A separate system, Auto-review, checks certain planned actions against instructions and safety requirements. OpenAI says the agent cannot modify the controls enforcing those checks.

    "Dots can still make mistakes," the company cautions.

    Recent findings suggest that openAI's Dots system-card appendix acknowledges that persistence and multi-agent systems are not new. Its evaluations examine how continuing work affects authorization boundaries.

    In one test involving successive related tasks, moderate scope violations increased from 8.6% to 19.7% when the number of intervening tasks doubled from five to 10. Examples included carrying information between unrelated tasks or editing a shared document beyond the intended scope. The company reported no severe breaches or exfiltration in that evaluation.

    These are controlled test results, not measured failure rates in customer deployments. They nevertheless identify a problem that a successful demonstration cannot settle: whether an agent keeps the right boundaries as its workload accumulates.

    According to OpenAI's DevDay recap, Dots are available to Pro and Business Premium users in eligible markets. Enterprise, Edu, and Healthcare access is an administrator-enabled beta, off by default.

    Recent findings suggest that the operational question is how organizations will keep delegated authority current. A continuing assignment needs a human owner who can revise its scope and decide when to stop it. Otherwise, the convenience of leaving work with an agent can outlast the reason it was authorized.

    For more information, go to the OpenAI site.

    Sources indicate that john K. Waters is the editor in chief of a number of Converge360.com sites, with a focus on high-end development, AI and future tech. He's been writing about cutting-edge technologies and culture of Silicon Valley for more than two decades, and he's written more than a dozen books. He also co-scripted the documentary film Silicon Valley: A 100 Year Renaissance, which aired on PBS. He can be reached at [email protected].

    Microsoft has published a draft code of conduct that lays out how its homegrown AI models should behave, with human control taking priority over model capability, autonomy, and even task completion.

    AI is changing which human capabilities matter most at work, yet employees are reporting that some of those same capabilities are being eroded, according to a new study from IBM.

    Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

    AI agents have moved into mainstream enterprise use, but the content infrastructure needed to support them has struggled to keep up, according to a new report from cloud content management organization Box.

    #204011. Survey Identifies Data Governance Enforcement Gap for Agentic AI Tools

    📅 07 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (818 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Survey Identifies Data Governance Enforcement Gap for Agentic AI Tools

    📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to a new survey from identity security company Delinea, 99.7% of IT and security leaders said their organization has a formal policy governing what data AI tools and agents are permitted to access.
    • That disconnect is at the center of Delinea's fall 2026 Identity Security Report, "The AI Enforcement Gap," which suggests companies have made quick progress establishing AI governance but have not necessarily built the technical controls needed to enforce it.
    • The findings come from a pair of surveys covering 2,254 IT and security leaders and 2,250 non-IT employees at organizations with at least 500 employees across the U.S, U.K, Germany, Australia, Singapore, UAE, France, and India.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to a new survey from identity security company Delinea, 99.7% of IT and security leaders said their organization has a formal policy governing what data AI tools and agents are permitted to access. Yet only about 51% said AI access is checked against those policies in real time. Perhaps more worrying is that only 19% said their organization could detect in real time when an agent last accessed data outside its intended scope.

    That disconnect is at the center of Delinea's fall 2026 Identity Security Report, "The AI Enforcement Gap," which suggests companies have made quick progress establishing AI governance but have not necessarily built the technical controls needed to enforce it.

    The findings come from a pair of surveys covering 2,254 IT and security leaders and 2,250 non-IT employees at organizations with at least 500 employees across the U.S, U.K, Germany, Australia, Singapore, UAE, France, and India.

    All the organizations were using or piloting AI, while the employees surveyed used at least one AI tool for work.

    The problem becomes more consequential as companies move from AI tools that primarily respond to consumers toward agents capable of taking actions on their behalf.

    Eighty-seven percent of IT and security respondents noted their organization had experienced or suspected of an incident during the past year in which an AI tool or agent accessed sensitive information beyond what was required for its task.

    According to recent reports, delinea's research also suggests companies are giving agents access that can persist longer than necessary. Only 58% of IT and security leaders said they have mechanisms that automatically revoke or expire AI access when a session ends, and those controls do not necessarily cover every agent or tool. Forty-two percent said many agent credentials remain active until an audit.

    Agents also are not always receiving their own narrowly defined permissions. Half of IT leaders said their organizations use the employee's existing permissions as a boundary for what an agent can access. That can effectively hand an agent years of accumulated access belonging to the person who rolled out it.

    Sources indicate that that is particularly significant because an AI agent does not necessarily behave like a traditional service account. A service account typically performs a predefined process, while an agent can choose different tools, actions and sequences at runtime depending on the situation.

    Sources indicate that "Service accounts run fixed scripts," said Mike Albrecht, associate director in the Risk Advisory Practice at Cross Country Consulting. "An AI agent decides what actions it's going to take at runtime.".

    The enforcement problem is not limited to autonomous agents.

    According to recent reports, the researchers found that 76% of employees surveyed had bypassed formal approval at some point to use AI tools with tech giant data, applications or systems. And 48% mentioned they always or extensively use AI tools without going through formal approval.

    Meanwhile, 60% stated they had felt pressure to use AI with sensitive or confidential information even when they were not sure doing so was permitted.

    Executives were particularly likely to circumvent the process. Eighty-one percent of C-level respondents stated they always or regularly bypass AI access approval, compared with 33% of intermediate-level employees.

    The result is a widening gap between written AI governance and what companies can see and control. Delinea found that only 41% of IT leaders remarked all AI tools and agents accessing company data are actively monitored. When an AI tool or agent went outside its intended scope, 55% said it took at least a day to detect the incident, while 30% said detection took four days or longer.

    That suggests the next phase of enterprise AI governance may depend less on writing additional rules and more on whether organizations can enforce existing ones while an agent is working.

    Industry observers note that "Most organizations cannot confidently answer three questions: What agents are running in our environment? What can they access? What have they actually done?" mentioned Delinea CEO Art Gilliland. "An agent can begin a session with legitimate access and drift into something it was never meant to do.".

    The full report is available for download here.

    Microsoft has published a draft code of conduct that lays out how its homegrown AI models should behave, with human control taking priority over model capability, autonomy, and even task completion.

    AI is changing which human capabilities matter most at work, yet employees are reporting that some of those same capabilities are being eroded, according to a new study from IBM.

    Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

    AI agents have moved into mainstream enterprise use, but the content infrastructure needed to support them has struggled to keep up, according to a newly introduced report from cloud content management tech giant Box.

    Claude Intros Sonnet 5.5 with Model-Switching Cybersecurity Safeguards

    📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that anthropic's new Claude release, Sonnet 5.5, brings cybersecurity safeguards that can change which model handles a request during a Claude conversation.
    • It has been revealed that according to Anthropic's explanation of model switching, automatic fallback is enabled by default in Claude.
    • The company identifies penetration testing and exploit generation among activities that may trigger cybersecurity fallbacks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that anthropic's new Claude release, Sonnet 5.5, brings cybersecurity safeguards that can change which model handles a request during a Claude conversation. Higher-risk tasks can fall back to Sonnet 5.

    It has been revealed that according to Anthropic's explanation of model switching, automatic fallback is enabled by default in Claude. Users receive a notice, and the answer is labeled with the model that provided it. The chat then stays on Sonnet 5 unless the user changes the selection.

    The company identifies penetration testing and exploit generation among activities that may trigger cybersecurity fallbacks. Source-code vulnerability scanning remains supported. Biology and reasoning-extraction safeguards can block requests outright, rather than route them elsewhere.

    The distinction matters operationally. A block stops the request; a fallback allows an attempt to continue with a different model. Neither outcome should be treated as interchangeable with completion by the model the user originally chose.

    Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 generates output more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and can reduce cost per task by up to 30%, based on its testing. Token prices remain unchanged.

    In a recent development, those claims describe performance under the firm's test conditions. An organization evaluating the service also needs to examine what happens when its own assignments encounter safeguards.

    It has been revealed that an internal pilot could record how often work is interrupted, whether fallback answers are usable, and when customers need help. Such measurements would give buyers a more relevant basis for deployment than assuming every task receives the advertised model's capabilities.

    Recent findings suggest that anthropic has confirmed intends to expand its Cyber Verification Program with tiered access for Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Mythos models. Its current program guidance explicitly excludes the two fresh 5.5 models and indicates the expansion is forthcoming.

    Organizations should distinguish those planned arrangements from access available today.

    The broader enterprise matter is accountability. When an AI service changes models during an assignment, someone still needs to determine whether the resulting work is suitable. A visible handoff helps, but organizations must decide how employees should respond to it.

    For more information on Sonnet 5.5, go to the Anthropic site.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures.
    • The research, conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global, examines both the risks and potential benefits of the technologies.
    • In a recent development, cloud-based storage, cloud-delivered applications, and cloud management infrastructure were the three most frequently cited asset types targeted by attackers, at 35%, 34%, and 32%, respectively.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures. The 2026 Thales Data Threat Report: Quantum & AI Trends, based on responses from 3,120 security and IT management professionals across 20 countries, found that 98% are considering how the two technologies affect each other. Thirty percent reported a significant increase in security budgets specifically for AI.

    The research, conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global, examines both the risks and potential benefits of the technologies. Fifty-seven percent believe quantum computing will enhance machine learning, while 54% expect it to enable advanced simulations of complex systems. The security findings span data governance, cloud infrastructure, and preparations for quantum-resistant encryption.

    In a recent development, cloud-based storage, cloud-delivered applications, and cloud management infrastructure were the three most frequently cited asset types targeted by attackers, at 35%, 34%, and 32%, respectively. The report connects that exposure to the large datasets required for AI training and the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

    Industry observers note that organizations are also looking to cloud providers for protection: 67% reported investing in their cloud provider's AI-specific security tools, compared with 63% using an established security provider. Respondents could identify multiple sources of protection, including startups, large language model providers, and internally developed controls.

    In a recent development, encryption coverage remains incomplete. Only 7% of organizations reported encrypting more than 80% of their sensitive cloud data, while 29% reported encrypting more than 60%. The report's chart puts the average share encrypted at 47% in 2026, down from 51% in 2025.

    The findings extend concerns raised in coverage of Thales' 2025 cloud security research, when AI security already ranked second to cloud security in spending priorities and 52% of respondents reported that AI security spending was displacing existing security budgets. The latest report again places AI security second, while its historical comparison shows average sensitive cloud data encryption coverage falling from 51% in 2025 to 47% in 2026.

    Industry observers note that AI security was the second-highest prioritized security spending category overall, behind cloud security. But protecting data ranked much lower among the measures organizations use to judge AI projects: Reducing or managing risks of data loss or noncompliance placed sixth among seven success criteria, at 35%.

    Improving customer experience led those measures at 68%, followed by reducing employee toil through greater task automation at 63%. Meanwhile, poor data quality or initial data governance was the leading inhibitor to AI adoption, cited by 65%; security risks from exposed data followed at 61%. Another 51% cited AI initiatives moving too promptly to be properly secured.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, cybersecurity company Flashpoint announced it has received U.S.
    • The patent comes at a time when security teams are confronting a growing vulnerability problem: Flashpoint's Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition tracked 21,667 vulnerability disclosures during the first half of 2026, an 8% increase.
    • According to recent reports, of those, 4,015, or around 19 percent, already had public or functional exploit code.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, cybersecurity company Flashpoint announced it has received U.S. Patent No. 12,705,360 for its Ransomware Risk model, a methodology designed to help security teams determine which newly disclosed vulnerabilities more closely resemble those historically used in ransomware attacks.

    The patent comes at a time when security teams are confronting a growing vulnerability problem: Flashpoint's Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition tracked 21,667 vulnerability disclosures during the first half of 2026, an 8% increase.

    According to recent reports, of those, 4,015, or around 19 percent, already had public or functional exploit code. Flashpoint also reported a 45 percent increase in Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) attacks during the period.

    The patent was granted August 11 2026, although the underlying Ransomware Risk model isn't new. It has been available through Flashpoint Vulnerability Intelligence since 2022.

    The model addresses a basic vulnerability-management problem: severity and real-world ransomware risk aren't necessarily the same thing, because severity scores do not necessarily indicate which flaws attackers are most likely to target.

    It has been revealed that the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, or CVSS, measures how severe a vulnerability could be. The Exploit Prediction Scoring System, or EPSS, estimates the probability of exploitation more broadly.

    Flashpoint's Ransomware Risk model adds another dimension by comparing newly disclosed vulnerabilities with the characteristics of flaws previously exploited in ransomware attacks.

    It has been revealed that that could change where a vulnerability lands in an organization's patching queue. A lower-severity flaw might normally sit behind numerous critical vulnerabilities. But if its characteristics closely resemble vulnerabilities repeatedly targeted by ransomware operators, security teams may have reason to move it higher.

    "A severity score alone can't tell you which vulnerabilities pose the greatest real-world risk of exploitation by ransomware actors," Flashpoint CEO Josh Lefkowitz stated. "Our patented Ransomware Risk model applies years of threat intelligence to that problem, giving customers an earlier signal and helping them prioritize based on how attackers actually operate.".

    The firm's midyear research also illustrates the scale of the prioritization problem. Its vulnerability intelligence covers traditional IT systems as well as cloud, IoT, operational technology, open source software. and third-party libraries.

    The company says it also tracks more than 105,000 vulnerabilities that aren't represented in CVE or the National Vulnerability Database, expanding the pool of flaws that security teams may need to evaluate.

    The cybersecurity organization's patented methodology profiles vulnerabilities using more than 60 technical characteristics, including whether a flaw can be exploited remotely without authentication, whether it affects operational technology systems, and how exploitation could affect data availability.

    Those characteristics form a multi-factor fingerprint. The model maps each vulnerability against clusters containing flaws previously exploited in ransomware attacks and assigns a Low, Medium, High, or Critical Ransomware Risk rating.

    Flashpoint indicates the rating can be generated when a vulnerability is disclosed, rather than requiring security teams to wait for public evidence of active exploitation. Ratings are then updated as new ransomware activity and threat intelligence emerge.

    Sources indicate that within Flashpoint Ignite, Ransomware Risk appears alongside CVSS, EPSS, Social Risk, and exploit maturity. The idea isn't to replace existing scoring systems, but to give administrators additional information when deciding what to remediate first.

    Sources indicate that nor does a High or Critical Ransomware Risk rating mean a vulnerability will necessarily be exploited. The model measures how closely its characteristics resemble vulnerabilities historically associated with ransomware attacks.

    According to recent reports, for security teams facing thousands of potential vulnerabilities, that distinction matters. The flaw carrying the highest severity score isn't necessarily the one that most closely resembles what ransomware operators have historically chosen to attack.

    "Despite being the most popular indicator for priority, we know that severity alone doesn't tell you whether a vulnerability will be exploited or used in ransomware," noted Ben Haynes, Data Science & Analytics Lead at Flashpoint and co-inventor of the patented methodology.

    "A vulnerability can score low on a traditional severity scale and still share the characteristics we repeatedly see in ransomware attacks.".

    For more information, go to the Flashpoint site.

    SailPoint Intros Newly introduced Capabilities to Address Agentic AI Identity Security Challenge

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, AI agents are moving from experiments into everyday enterprise environments, but the security controls around them are not keeping pace, according to enterprise identity security company SailPoint.
    • According to recent reports, that gap could become harder to ignore as organizations give agents more autonomy.
    • SailPoint, which develops identity security and access governance technology for enterprises, is responding with a collection of latest identity security capabilities revealed at its Navigate 2026 conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, AI agents are moving from experiments into everyday enterprise environments, but the security controls around them are not keeping pace, according to enterprise identity security company SailPoint. In its latest Horizons of Identity Security report, SailPoint found that 79% of enterprises already have AI agents running in production, while just 2% have deployed identity security tools specifically designed to govern them.

    According to recent reports, that gap could become harder to ignore as organizations give agents more autonomy. Agents can increasingly access applications, sensitive data, and credentials, and in some cases take actions on a user's behalf, effectively creating a new class of identity that IT and security teams need to manage.

    SailPoint, which develops identity security and access governance technology for enterprises, is responding with a collection of latest identity security capabilities revealed at its Navigate 2026 conference. The firm is expanding its Agentic Fabric to discover "shadow AI" agents and provide runtime authorization and controls capable of immediately disabling an agent.

    The firm also introduced what it calls SailPoint Autonomous Agents, specialized AI agents designed to govern other agents. The security agents can monitor runtime activity, intercept threats, and adjust permissions while allowing legitimate agents to continue operating, SailPoint said.

    The idea reflects one of the challenges created by increasingly autonomous AI systems: Traditional human approval processes may not be fast enough to govern software capable of taking large numbers of actions on its own.

    "The idea that a security admin is going to review and approve access for a group of autonomous agents making 10,000 tool calls a second isn't just outdated — it's a fantasy," SailPoint CTO Chandra Gnanasambandam stated.

    Another part of SailPoint's approach focuses on visibility.

    Fresh endpoint and browser sensors, along with SIEM and XDR telemetry and non-human identity discovery capabilities, are designed to uncover agents, MCP servers, credentials, tools, and data stores that haven't been brought under an organization's identity program.

    It has been revealed that the manufacturer is also introducing Autonomous Identity Security Posture Management, or A-ISPM, which uses identity information from its Atlas platform to identify dormant accounts, orphaned access, shadow administrators, and other potentially risky access paths. Organizations can then revoke access, disable an identity or AI agent, assign an owner or automate enforcement.

    Just-in-Time provisioning is another part of the strategy. Rather than giving people, service accounts, and AI agents permanent access, permissions can be granted when needed and subjected to conditions such as reauthentication or a business justification.

    Capabilities across SailPoint's Agentic Fabric, Human Fabric, and Atlas platforms are beginning to roll out globally. A-ISPM and several other announced features are expected in the company's fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.

    "Autonomous agents are no longer just experimental copilots; they are becoming the primary execution layer of modern enterprises," SailPoint President Matt Mills said.

    For more information, go to the SailPoint site.

    Microsoft has published a draft code of conduct that lays out how its homegrown AI models should behave, with human control taking priority over model capability, autonomy, and even task completion.

    AI is changing which human capabilities matter most at work, yet employees are reporting that some of those same capabilities are being eroded, according to a upcoming study from IBM.

    Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

    AI agents have moved into mainstream enterprise use, but the content infrastructure needed to support them has struggled to keep up, according to a new report from cloud content management company Box.

    #203977. Survey: Most Organizations Are Not Consistently Measuring AI Value Against Costs

    📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (594 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Survey: Most Organizations Are Not Consistently Measuring AI Value Against Costs

    📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A upcoming study from consulting firm KPMG found that while AI investment continues to grow, relatively few organizations consistently measure whether the technology's benefits justify its costs.
    • Average planned AI investment for the next 12 months has risen to $210 million, compared with $186 million in the first quarter of 2026.
    • The findings are based on responses from 2,131 senior leaders across 20 countries and jurisdictions, surveyed between July 23 and August 26, 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A upcoming study from consulting firm KPMG found that while AI investment continues to grow, relatively few organizations consistently measure whether the technology's benefits justify its costs. The organization's Global AI Pulse Q3 2026 report found that 89% of organizations report measurable value from AI, while just 12% consistently assess that value against costs across the organization.

    Average planned AI investment for the next 12 months has risen to $210 million, compared with $186 million in the first quarter of 2026.

    The findings are based on responses from 2,131 senior leaders across 20 countries and jurisdictions, surveyed between July 23 and August 26, 2026.

    Most organizations have established ways to track AI spending: 61% review costs during project approval, and 59% monitor them once systems are operating.

    Consistently connecting those costs to value remains less common. Beyond the 12% that do so across the organization, another 26% assess value against costs for most initiatives.

    According to recent reports, organizations reporting established AI returns have stronger measurement practices. Among this group, 48% consistently assess value against costs, four times the proportion in the overall survey group.

    Cost-monitoring dashboards are also more common among organizations reporting established returns: 77% use them, compared with 43% of those still experimenting.

    Industry observers note that "The organizations seeing a return did the implementation and the transformation properly: guardrails in place, workforce ready, data cleaned up," said Priya Emmanuel, global head of aIQ at KPMG International. "That is a sequence, not a secret.".

    Organizations are also developing more formal systems to manage AI deployment.

    Fifty-five percent operate a formal AI management layer, which KPMG calls a "harness layer," comprising controls and tools between AI models and business applications.

    In a recent development, security and identity controls, along with data access controls, were the most common capabilities, each reported by 43% of respondents. Model routing, which determines which model handles a particular task, was reported by 23%.

    Meanwhile, 53% assign accountability for AI-informed decisions to a named executive, the CEO, or an executive committee.

    The proportion reporting significant employee adoption of AI agents rose from 25% in the first quarter to 34% in the third quarter.

    Cybersecurity concerns were more common among organizations with mature AI programs.

    Half of those reporting established AI returns identified cybersecurity as a barrier, compared with roughly one-third of those still experimenting.

    Overall, 86% of respondents said their organizations are adapting their cybersecurity operating models to address AI-accelerated threats.

    The report identifies accountability, operational resilience, and cost management as priorities as AI becomes more embedded in business operations.

    "Many organizations have made AI models widely available and track their use," said Swaminathan Chandrasekaran, head of the US AI Center of Excellence at KPMG. "But consumption alone is not a strategy.".

    For the full report, visit the KPMG site.

    Microsoft has published a draft code of conduct that lays out how its homegrown AI models should behave, with human control taking priority over model capability, autonomy, and even task completion.

    AI is changing which human capabilities matter most at work, yet employees are reporting that some of those same capabilities are being eroded, according to a latest study from IBM.

    Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

    AI agents have moved into mainstream enterprise use, but the content infrastructure needed to support them has struggled to keep up, according to a latest report from cloud content management organization Box.

    #203971. Report: Cyber Attacks Increasingly Exploit Trusted Workplace Tools

    📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (683 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Report: Cyber Attacks Increasingly Exploit Trusted Workplace Tools

    📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In its latest threat intelligence report, Ontinue found that attackers are increasingly using trusted workplace tools to trick customers into giving them access to enterprise networks.
    • Ontinue's report notes the trouble is that these attacks blend in with ordinary workday communication, which makes them harder to catch.
    • In a recent development, "The majority of effective attacks today don't rely on sophisticated exploits.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In its latest threat intelligence report, Ontinue found that attackers are increasingly using trusted workplace tools to trick customers into giving them access to enterprise networks. Approximately 30% of organizations monitored by the cybersecurity firm experienced at least one attempt to impersonate IT support through Microsoft Teams during the first half of 2026. About one in every 990 external Teams contacts highlighted signs of someone pretending to be an internal IT worker.

    Ontinue's report notes the trouble is that these attacks blend in with ordinary workday communication, which makes them harder to catch.

    In a recent development, "The majority of effective attacks today don't rely on sophisticated exploits. They rely on trust," Balazs Greksza, director of Advanced Threat Operations at Ontinue, noted in the company's announcement.

    Ontinue broke down how a typical attack works: An employee gets an unexpected Teams message or call from someone claiming to work in the organization's IT department. The person warns of a security problem, a software problem or an enhancement that can't wait. Then they walk the employee through opening Windows Quick Assist, installing remote-access software, or running a PowerShell command. Following those steps can hand the attacker control of the employee's computer, often without the employee realizing it.

    It has been revealed that the approach is very similar to the Black Basta ransomware group, which helped popularize similar attacks in 2024. Unfortunately, Ontinue found the technique has since been adopted by other cybercriminal groups, including some with no known link to Black Basta.

    Industry observers note that some threat agents are also combining tactics. They might first overwhelm an employee's inbox with unwanted e-mails, then reach out through Teams pretending to be IT support offering to fix the problem.

    It has been revealed that "Phishing no longer resides solely in your inbox. It has spread across the entire corporate communications environment," mentioned Mika Aalto, co-founder and CEO of Hoxhunt.

    Industry observers note that teams impersonation is only part of the problem. Ontinue also found attackers taking advantage of legitimate Microsoft sign-in processes. Between May and June, researchers identified 10 confirmed device-code phishing compromises across five customer tenants.

    In these attacks, criminals trick employees into completing what appears to be a normal Microsoft authentication process. But doing so can give the attacker access to the employee's account and system without actually breaking their password.

    The report also found attackers using blockchain-based infrastructure to hide malicious activity, accounting for more than 25% of confirmed malicious ClickFix findings.

    "Attackers are no longer looking for gaps in your perimeter. They are looking for the systems your organization already trusts and finding ways to move through them undetected," mentioned Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

    The security firm indicates that IT needs to keep a closer eye on unexpected Teams contacts, remote-support requests, suspicious PowerShell activity, and changes to authentication settings. Employees should also confirm sensitive requests through established internal channels, rather than relying on the name or account that appears on their screen.

    Aviv Nahum, co-founder and CEO of Above Security, noted that AI is making these attacks more convincing by helping criminals imitate familiar voices, writing styles, and conversations.

    "The security model therefore must shift from 'does this look real?' to 'can I independently verify that this person is who they claim to be?'" Nahum noted.

    The full Ontinue report can be found here.

    Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Unauthorized artificial intelligence tools and agents are creating security risks for organizations as AI adoption increases, according to cybersecurity tech giant Sophos.
    • Separate research from Gartner and Cloud Security Alliance found that 82% of organizations discovered shadow AI agents in their environments during the previous year.
    • According to the security firm, organizations have struggled to identify which AI tools employees use, what information those tools access, and whether their use complies with security policies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Unauthorized artificial intelligence tools and agents are creating security risks for organizations as AI adoption increases, according to cybersecurity tech giant Sophos. In a recent product announcement, the company highlighted the growing use of shadow AI, referring to AI tools and agents operating without formal organizational approval or oversight. The security firm cited research indicating that 69% of organizations suspect or have evidence of unauthorized AI use.

    Separate research from Gartner and Cloud Security Alliance found that 82% of organizations discovered shadow AI agents in their environments during the previous year.

    According to the security firm, organizations have struggled to identify which AI tools employees use, what information those tools access, and whether their use complies with security policies.

    "Organizations are adopting AI faster than they can secure it, and most security teams can't answer three basic questions: which AI tools are running, what data is going into them, and whether that activity lines up with policy," stated Kyle Falkenhagen, senior vice president of product management at Sophos.

    The manufacturer also cited an IDC projection that the number of AI agents could reach 1.3 billion by 2028.

    Sophos researchers reported observing attackers use AI agents within a customer's network to build and test nearly 80 malware modules.

    The cybersecurity firm declared the general availability of Sophos AI Defense, a security offering designed to identify AI tools, monitor their activity, and enforce organizational security policies.

    The product operates through Sophos Fusion, the firm's cybersecurity platform, and uses information from devices, networks, identity systems, and browsers.

    According to the company, AI Defense can inspect prompts, uploads, and other AI interactions to identify potentially risky activity and help prevent sensitive data exposure.

    For more information, go to the Sophos site.

    Microsoft has published a draft code of conduct that lays out how its homegrown AI models should behave, with human control taking priority over model capability, autonomy, and even task completion.

    Microsoft Expands AI Security Platform to Address Agentic AI Security Risks

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Microsoft is expanding the scope of its AI-powered Project Perception security platform to address the growing concern that AI agents may have access to sensitive information and systems, yet don't always behave as expected.
    • In a company blog post, Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, outlined how Microsoft prepares to use Project Perception to monitor, manage, and contain what it calls "agentic insiders." These are AI agents deployed within an environment that can access data, use software tools, and make decisions without constant human supervision.
    • "Agents are unpredictable," Gallot wrote.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Microsoft is expanding the scope of its AI-powered Project Perception security platform to address the growing concern that AI agents may have access to sensitive information and systems, yet don't always behave as expected.

    In a company blog post, Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, outlined how Microsoft prepares to use Project Perception to monitor, manage, and contain what it calls "agentic insiders." These are AI agents deployed within an environment that can access data, use software tools, and make decisions without constant human supervision. While they can improve productivity, Microsoft warns that they also introduce security risks, even when they haven't been compromised by an attacker.

    "Agents are unpredictable," Gallot wrote. "They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended, and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised.".

    Recent findings suggest that project Perception was first introduced in July. The platform, which entered public preview Aug. 3, is designed to help security teams respond to increasingly sophisticated cyber threats using AI-powered automation.

    In a recent development, instead of leaning only on traditional security alerts and manual investigations, Project Perception uses three kinds of specialized AI agents working together. Red team agents hunt for possible vulnerabilities, blue team agents look into suspicious activity, and green team agents step in to fix problems and strengthen defenses.

    To spot threats and respond faster, the system pulls in security data from identities, endpoints, cloud environments, applications, and other sources.

    Now Microsoft wants to use those same capabilities on the AI agents already running inside enterprise networks. Project Perception would find those agents, give them identities and permissions, and keep an eye on what they do across different systems. It would also keep assessing the risks that come with their actions.

    Sources indicate that microsoft also described a blueprint for "Guardian Agents," specialized AI agents that supervise other agents and step in when their behavior gets risky. That might mean limiting an agent's permissions or blocking certain actions before they cause harm.

    "Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous," Gallot wrote.

    The initiative also reflects concerns raised by Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella in an Oct. 10 essay on AI security.

    Nadella argued that enterprises should treat powerful AI models much like potential insider security risks, particularly when those models can access confidential information or perform critical business operations.

    "We simply can't outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf," Nadella wrote.

    He called for security controls that operate independently of AI models, including restricted permissions, detailed activity logging, and mechanisms that allow administrators to stop an agent's actions.

    "In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it," Nadella wrote.

    Microsoft admits that watching what AI agents do is only part of the answer. Gallot stated that future security tools will also need to show why AI models make the choices they do, not just what actions they end up taking.

    For more information, go to the Microsoft blog.

    Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

    Microsoft has published a draft code of conduct that lays out how its homegrown AI models should behave, with human control taking priority over model capability, autonomy, and even task completion.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to a survey by data and AI services provider Further, enterprises are reporting benefits from artificial intelligence even as their data preparation and oversight processes remain incomplete.
    • In a recent development, the tech giant's recent State of Enterprise AI Maturity research surveyed 515 U.S.-based AI decision-makers.
    • The findings suggest that gaining value from individual AI applications and preparing to operate them more broadly are separate challenges.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to a survey by data and AI services provider Further, enterprises are reporting benefits from artificial intelligence even as their data preparation and oversight processes remain incomplete.

    In a recent development, the tech giant's recent State of Enterprise AI Maturity research surveyed 515 U.S.-based AI decision-makers. Just 5% believed their organizations' data was largely ready for AI.

    The findings suggest that gaining value from individual AI applications and preparing to operate them more broadly are separate challenges. Reported returns alone do not establish that an organization has the foundations to sustain or expand those results.

    It has been revealed that further found that 37% of respondents' organizations had paused, scaled back, or abandoned an underperforming AI initiative in the previous 12 months. Among that group, data quality or availability was the most frequently cited main reason, at 24%.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, 29% reported completing a formal data audit and remediation blueprint. The research also placed 69% of organizations in the exploring, experimenting, or implementing stages of adoption.

    Further distinguishes data prepared for conventional reporting from data prepared for AI. Its explanation emphasizes data origins and documentation, along with access controls that support ongoing evaluation and governance.

    Sources indicate that for readers assessing their own readiness, the practical problem is whether data supports the requirements of a particular application. A collection suitable for a dashboard may need additional preparation before it can reliably support an AI system.

    Seventy-seven percent reported a positive return on AI investment. However, only 3% noted their organizations had a documented AI-audit process.

    Sources indicate that the findings measure different things: perceived financial benefit and the existence of a repeatable oversight process. Neither substitutes for the other.

    Sources indicate that "In reality, confidence without a documented process is exposure," stated Kierra Dotson, associate director of AI strategy and governance at Further. "Closing that gap doesn't take newly introduced technology; it requires an auditable governance process.".

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Inside a Modern Hamptons Home With Views in Nearly Every Direction

    📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
