    Is This the Ultimate Aspen Anti-Chalet?

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Above: The primary bathroom of a home in Aspen, Colorado, designed by Rafael de Cárdenas with architecture by SAOTA.
    • “We’re having a crisis of taste,” architect and designer Rafael de Cárdenas is in the midst of saying.
    • According to recent reports, so when longtime client Rachel Dorrell asked him to create a mountain house in Aspen for her growing family, no one expected a typical ski chalet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Above: The primary bathroom of a home in Aspen, Colorado, designed by Rafael de Cárdenas with architecture by SAOTA. Custom tub with Dornbracht fittings; ceramic vase by artist Kazunori Hamana; side table by Rafael Prieto.

    “We’re having a crisis of taste,” architect and designer Rafael de Cárdenas is in the midst of saying. “There’s a sameness. It’s all a historical mishmash.” He’s at breakfast in Manhattan drinking a cinnamon latte (the restaurant did not have the turmeric he requested). He has already completed his run in Central Park and his gratitude list in his Day One journal app, and he’s on day 735 following a visit to the Hoffman Institute—the famously mysterious weeklong “personal growth” retreat. “I feel like we’re in The Handmaid’s Tale,” he indicates. “AI is happening, but we’re going to pretend we’re designing manor houses in the English countryside in the 19th century?” Later he adds, “I have never been interested in recreating the past.”.

    According to recent reports, so when longtime client Rachel Dorrell asked him to create a mountain house in Aspen for her growing family, no one expected a typical ski chalet. From her first visit to the plot of land, she realized the views of the town and the slopes beyond would be unmatched. Today those “crazy views” are framed by windows so large it’s hard to tell where rooms end and the outside begins. De Cárdenas, who collaborated with SAOTA architects to create the modernist structure, set about realizing Dorrell’s vision of “Colorado, but refined,” as she puts it. “Glamorous ’80s apartment” is how he describes the results.

    In a recent development, “The mood board was Angelo Donghia,” that great of American design who worked with the likes of Liza Minnelli. “And Beetlejuice, always Beetlejuice! And Mickey Rourke’s apartment in 91/2 Weeks.” A cheetah-print rug sits in the library, while sculpted white custom sofas anchor the immense yet minimalist living room. “So many people have asked, ‘Shouldn’t there be art above the fireplace?’ ” de Cárdenas states. “I’m like, ‘Why?’ ”.

    Sources indicate that following the rules has never been his style. It has been 20 years since he released his design firm, after studying at UCLA and assisting architect Greg Lynn at Vienna’s Angewandte institute and MAK museum, then returning to his native Upcoming York. The son of an erstwhile fashion PR executive and an actuary, de Cárdenas aspired to work for David Rockwell or for Alex de Betak’s fashion production company, where he once applied for a job. In the end he did a stint at Calvin Klein and worked as a production designer for films and commercials. Then a friend asked for help redoing a kitchen, something he did “kind of at night,” de Cárdenas remembers. Next came his first real client: actress Parker Posey. It was a revelation. “She was the first person I ever had to make window treatments for. I was like, ‘What the f***?’ I remember looking at a window and being like, ‘What is this supposed to look like?’ I didn’t understand that residential interior design is, essentially, fabric.”.

    Sources indicate that around the same time, he landed his first major corporate client, Nike, and did the design of aNYthing, a Lower East Side boutique that became a nexus for skaters, artists, and musicians in the late 2000s. “No one was doing stores like that at the time,” says creative director Jen Brill, who worked with de Cárdenas on several Nike projects. “There was nothing minimal about it. It was loud, it was fun. It was the first store I saw that was like retail theater.”.

    Recent findings suggest that another friend, Felix Burrichter, a curator and the founder of Pin-Up architecture magazine, recalls de Cárdenas’s early fascination with the Memphis Group architects (“when it was still considered bad taste,” Burrichter says) as well as his willingness to experiment with materials, such as applying duct tape patterns to the walls of a Jeffrey Deitch exhibition in Rome, or wrapping an Ikea chair with fluorescent gaffer tape. “For the aNYthing store, I physically built a lot of those things, because there was no one to do it and no budget,” de Cárdenas says. He sometimes laments not being so hands-on anymore, now that he has a team of 18 based in New York and Paris. “There was a lot of energy in those projects.”.

    “His work is like Limelight–meets–Park Avenue,” notes Burrichter, who calls de Cárdenas the heir to ELLE Decor A-List designer Peter Marino, a maestro who works with significant private clients alongside luxury behemoths such as Dior and Chanel. De Cárdenas may have moved from duct tape to gold leaf applied by European artisans, “but there is always that tension in Raf’s work,” Burrichter says, “the binary between decorating and being an architect, between uptown and the club.”.

    In a recent development, dorrell, for her part, became aware of de Cárdenas a decade ago, when she and her husband purchased a home in the West Village that he had staged. “We were like, ‘Who did the interiors and who did the art? It’s perfect.’ ” She indicates they were drawn to the ’70s vibe and the peachy hues, an unusual shade at the time. “We didn’t change a thing.” Since then they have worked together on homes in Austin, New York, and currently their largest yet, in Palm Beach. Dorrell sends “rapid-fire” texts of inspiration ranging from tiled walls at Lake Como’s Villa d’Este to barstools in Paris. “Raf cracks me up—we are brutally honest with each other,” she says, explaining that her taste skews more traditional, while his is often edgier.

    “Some of my projects have moments that are ugly, and they excite me,” he states. “Because something truly excellent, something that is pushing boundaries, is not going to land pleasurably at first.” He points to Madonna, a frequent touchstone and source of inspiration for him. “The first time you saw Blond Ambition, the first time you saw Madonna with a high ponytail and with the headset, it was a little jarring. The thick eyebrow and the cone bra.” He often finds himself thinking, Where is that moment now?

    According to recent reports, despite his concerns about the flattening effect of the algorithm, he’s still happy he’s in the business of taste. “I can’t believe I was lucky enough to land here, because I didn’t know what interior design even was,” he notes. “I like my job. I’m grateful for my job. I want people to say, ‘He’s good at his job.’ ”.

    In a recent development, the Dorrells might concur: “ ‘We’re not doing another project,’ ” Rachel recalls her husband saying about Aspen. “Now he’s like, ‘Thank god,’ because it’s so awesome.”.

    This story originally appeared in the November 2026 glitch of ELLE Decor.

    #203895. Breaking: Does Anyone Care How Yellowjackets Ends Anymore?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (900 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Does Anyone Care How Yellowjackets Ends Anymore?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Believe it or not, Yellowjackets is based on real events.
    • Recent findings suggest that yellowjackets, in a way, explores what might have happened had the group never revealed just how they managed to survive in the wilderness.
    • In a recent development, the series explored survival in all its forms, from the lasting effects of grief to the need for women to escape their mundane, suburban lives for a little danger.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Believe it or not, Yellowjackets is based on real events. In 1972, a high school rugby team, along with their families, boarded Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571 and crashed in the Andes. Only sixteen of the forty-five passengers survived when they were rescued seventy-two days later, and they all harbored a dark secret: To survive, they ate the flesh of the people who had died.

    Recent findings suggest that yellowjackets, in a way, explores what might have happened had the group never revealed just how they managed to survive in the wilderness. Much like Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571, the Showtime series follows a high school women’s soccer team that survives a plane crash by killing and eating each other. Cocreators Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson blended in potential supernatural elements such as a dark presence that possibly forces them to kill, classic Lord of the Flies homages, and a killer soundtrack. Yellowjackets also cut ahead to each survivor’s life as an adult, featuring the acting talents of Melanie Lynskey, Christina Ricci, and Juliette Lewis. For a while, it was engrossing TV.

    In a recent development, the series explored survival in all its forms, from the lasting effects of grief to the need for women to escape their mundane, suburban lives for a little danger. It was critically acclaimed, nominated for awards, and topped many “Best of the Year” lists. But then, five years and two more chaotic seasons went by that really seemed to test its audience’s … well, appetites.

    Now that the fourth and final season is upon us—season 4 premiered on Friday, November 20—the answers to Yellowjackets’ burning questions will finally be revealed. Namely: Is something forcing them to kill each other, or can everything be explained by science? Will the public find out that they resorted to ritualistic murder and cannibalism? And, most importantly, is there anyone left who’s still interested in finding out?

    Industry observers note that to be fair, there’s already something of an answer to that last question. Despite critical fatigue for the series, over two million viewers tuned in to the season 3 premiere last year, per Paramount. That number then increased a bit to 3 million by the season 3 finale. Sure, those numbers pale in comparison to The Pitt season 2’s 15.4 million average weekly viewers or even the Landman season 2 premiere’s 9.2 million viewers. But there is a fan base willing to see this series to the end, whatever happens.

    In a recent development, what is that ending? Where the series right now stands, our girls are finally returning home after being rescued. They’ll likely adjust to normal life again by committing another hunt back in their hometown. And in the present, the promise of “last one standing” in the pre-roll recap likely points to a final bloodbath. Is that even what fans want? Until that finale, how everything will resolve, and what it all really means, remains a mystery.

    According to recent reports, for the Uruguayans, they faced a moral and religious crisis when they returned. When news broke that the rugby team ate the flesh of their dead passengers, one of the survivors defended their actions by comparing it to that of Jesus Christ and the Eucharist. According to the survivor, the group made a pact to sacrifice their bodies for each other if they perished so that they could eat their flesh to survive. The media circus completely flipped, and they were heroes once again. Pope Paul VI even wrote them a letter to sanctify their actions. It’s a fascinating end to their story—but one that the Yellowjackets cocreators likely found made for an entirely different sort of TV show.

    According to recent reports, outside of the pagan imagery and supernatural threats that the Yellowjackets cast face, religion has yet to enter the picture. The cannibalism mostly seemed inevitable until it finally happened halfway through season 2, and besides that, the women have done much worse since returning home. After three seasons of one cold-blooded murder after another, the body count just to keep their secret hidden is enough for all of them to face the electric chair. And even if there is a malevolent force controlling them, it may take a metaphorical release of pain and grief on par with Hereditary or Weapons to fully satisfy viewers in the series finale.

    “To some extent, I do feel as though if we were to just 100 percent jump both feet on one side of [the supernatural/reality] line, it would disperse some of what makes this show interesting,” cocreator Ashley Lyle told CBR ahead of season 4.

    Industry observers note that “I think that we are fully aware that we are either going to delight or anger both sides of that equation in some way, shape, or form,” they added. “But I don’t know that that could have been avoided.”.

    At this point, some version of watching the women all kill each other, or even watching them all defeat the evil they believe is haunting them, just doesn’t feel like enough. The show’s biggest problem might have just been that it ran too long. A simpler ending to a shorter story might have left viewers delighted. But we shall see! If Yellowjackets can land the plane (sorry) in the end, I’m willing to eat (apologies again) my own words on this one.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sign-in problems account for up to 53% of help desk tickets at individual enterprises, but network complications can take significantly longer to resolve, according to a latest study from ControlUp.
    • Analyzing 1,069,110 help desk tickets, the IT operations firm identified password resets, account lockouts, and multifactor authentication (MFA) complications as major drivers of support demand.
    • At one large enterprise, account-related tickets took a median of 11 minutes to resolve, compared with 50 hours for network problems.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sign-in problems account for up to 53% of help desk tickets at individual enterprises, but network complications can take significantly longer to resolve, according to a latest study from ControlUp.

    Analyzing 1,069,110 help desk tickets, the IT operations firm identified password resets, account lockouts, and multifactor authentication (MFA) complications as major drivers of support demand.

    At one large enterprise, account-related tickets took a median of 11 minutes to resolve, compared with 50 hours for network problems. Meanwhile, 87% of network and phone tickets were reassigned between teams, compared with 20% of account tickets.

    MFA enrollment and re-enrollment problems appeared at 40% of organizations, with one in five linking these challenges to employees replacing or upgrading their phones. Virtual desktop problems appeared at 55% of organizations analyzed.

    Traditional phone support remained a major channel for IT assistance.

    In a recent development, among organizations that recorded how support requests were submitted, 57% reported that phone calls accounted for approximately two-thirds or more of contacts. At one organization, that figure reached 99%.

    Machine-generated tickets from monitoring, security, backup, and patching systems appeared at half of the organizations studied. At 15%, automated tickets represented between 25% and 50% of all requests.

    The research covered enterprises across retail, healthcare, financial services, manufacturing, construction, energy, and IT services.

    ControlUp noted the findings highlight the need to evaluate recurring problems and their operational impact rather than relying solely on ticket volume and resolution speed.

    "IT organizations have traditionally measured support performance by how promptly they close tickets, but that doesn't tell the whole story," noted Simon Townsend, senior vice president of marketing and office of the CTO at ControlUp.

    "A password reset that takes a few minutes and an infrastructure failure that disrupts an entire location shouldn't carry the same operational weight.".

    For more information, go to the ControlUp site.

    Industry News: This London Townhouse Was Designed for the Holidays

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that above: In the living room, the seating is by Luther Quintana with Samuel & Sons fringe.
    • It has been revealed that some homes are for summers by the water, others for weekends on the slopes.
    • Located near Richmond Park, in southwestern London, the 19th-century townhouse has been in Houser’s family for more than 20 years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that above: In the living room, the seating is by Luther Quintana with Samuel & Sons fringe. The wallcovering is by Iksel, and the cocktail table has a Fornasetti top.

    It has been revealed that some homes are for summers by the water, others for weekends on the slopes. When Krystyna Houser set about redecorating her family’s London townhouse, she was thinking of Christmas. “We spend every Christmas there,” she indicates. At this house, that meant more than just putting up a tree.

    Located near Richmond Park, in southwestern London, the 19th-century townhouse has been in Houser’s family for more than 20 years. It was always a place to return to while Houser, founder of the nutritional startup mBIOTA Elemental, and her husband Dan, a co-founder of Rockstar Games, were raising their three children in Latest York City. Dan had grown up nearby, and the ample greenspace that gives the area its name made it an appealing place to visit with a young family. The interiors, however, had never quite received their due.

    Houser turned to Miles Redd and David Kaihoi, the partners behind the Fresh York–based firm Redd Kaihoi. She had known Redd since 2012, when she hired him to decorate a Brooklyn Heights townhouse, and the two became friends. They have since worked on multiple houses together. For London she trusted the designers to craft the warm and celebratory atmosphere she craved. “I wanted it to be equally elegant, cozy, and family-oriented,” she indicates.

    Red and green were a natural starting point, as green already had the family’s allegiance. “It’s one of their favorite colors,” Redd notes. “So we leaned into that a lot.” Verdant hues appear in velvet, felt, and marble throughout, while the entrance hall is dressed in crimson. These were holiday colors with no intention of coming down in January, and Redd was going for sophistication rather than holiday kitsch. “I wanted romantic 19th-century elegance, the feeling that they’re stepping into a Merchant Ivory movie.”.

    Recent findings suggest that this approach suits a firm known for exuberant color and layered furnishings. Redd brings a sense of theater to traditional decorating, drawing on the work of such legendary designers as Billy Baldwin, Albert Hadley, and John Fowler and mixing lacquer, chintz, and bold geometric patterns. Before opening his practice in 1998, he trained with antiques dealer John Rosselli and decorator Bunny Williams. Kaihoi, a sculptor, joined the ELLE Decor A-List firm in 2008 and became a partner in 2019. Together the duo give grand rooms an ease and wit that keep formality in check.

    Houser considers “interior designer” an insufficient description for Redd and Kaihoi. “I feel like they are set curators,” she notes. She gave them considerable freedom, occasionally inviting them to surprise her with potential purchases. “I don’t think it’s my place to hinder creative expression, and, as a result, the rooms are just magical.”.

    It has been revealed that the house’s existing architecture gave that freedom some useful structure. “It had great English bones,” Redd states. He retained the original living room mantelpiece, library doors, and front door, while upstairs he and Kaihoi worked to restore character lost to earlier alterations that had stripped away 19th-century details. An excavation created additional basement space for a screening room and a ping-pong area, giving the family more places to gather and play.

    From first visit to completion, the project took the better part of an unhurried decade, with pauses for permits, the Covid pandemic, and other commitments along the way. All the while Redd and Kaihoi kept shopping at auctions, antiques stores, and fairs, which ensured that the rooms would have an accumulated character. The designers looked to the guards at Buckingham Palace for the entrance hall and main staircase, borrowing the red and gold of their uniforms for its matka silk walls trimmed with gold braiding. Beyond the hall, the green velvet–lined library opens into a living room papered to resemble a coromandel screen.

    Industry observers note that upstairs, the primary bedroom and a sitting area occupy a long, narrow space. Green felt screen dividers give the bed its own area in one corner without a wall breaking up the suite. “It’s all sort of one big bedsit, which is a very English notion,” Redd notes. A small painting of a parrot on one of the screens keeps Houser company at her bedside.

    The couple wanted their suite to feel like a luxurious hotel—inviting places to read and work, a comfortable bed, and a generously scaled bathroom—without sacrificing a sense of home. “You’ve ruined hotels for us,” Redd recalls Houser telling him of their previous work.

    Step Inside the Ultimate Christmas Retreat.

    But Houser’s favorite rooms are the ones that bring everyone together: the kitchen and the adjoining striped family room, which open onto the garden. It’s here where everyone gathers for meals and to relax. The connected spaces provide separate places to eat, play games, and watch television, allowing the family to spend time together even when everyone is doing something different.

    “Their design helps bring us together,” Houser says. “And that’s what it is. It’s a family home.”.

    This story originally appeared in the November 2026 problem of ELLE Decor.

    Enterprise AI Spending Outpaces Adoption Growth, Report Finds

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a fresh Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.
    • It has been revealed that the venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025.
    • A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a fresh Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.

    It has been revealed that the venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025. The share of enterprises paying for AI rose from 55% to 65%.

    A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.

    Menlo's methodology describes revenue figures as annualized run rates. The $176.8 billion estimate therefore should not be read as $176.8 billion already spent during the first nine months of 2026.

    The report also distinguishes unusually heavy spenders from the typical respondent. Average reported spending reached 4.7 times the prior year's level, while the median reached 2.2 times. That gap suggests a smaller group of large spenders drove the average substantially.

    In a recent development, the practical implication is that an industry growth figure may be a poor benchmark for an individual organization's budget. Buyers need to understand their own workload growth and the results it produces.

    "Agents are changing the economics of software," Menlo principal Derek Xiao remarked in the firm's announcement.

    Recent findings suggest that menlo reports that agents account for 80% of tokens on OpenRouter, a service providing access to multiple models. That measures activity on one platform, rather than all enterprise AI use. Token consumption also measures processing volume, rather than completed business outcomes.

    An agent that makes repeated attempts can consume more resources without delivering proportionately more value. For procurement teams, the relevant comparison is consequently the cost of completing acceptable work, including the review it requires.

    Industry observers note that menlo estimates that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google capture 69% of enterprise AI deployment spending. That measure is distinct from their shares of enterprise language-model API spending, a narrower category. The figures should not be used interchangeably.

    The report draws on a Morning Consult survey of nearly 400 U.S. enterprise decision-makers responsible for more than $4 billion in AI spending. Market totals are modeled estimates informed by surveys, public filings, and third-party reports. Menlo discloses investments in Anthropic and OpenRouter.

    A separate announcement from Information Services Group describes buyers putting more emphasis on the economics and reliability of production deployments. ISG says ongoing security and observability work remains necessary as organizations scale.

    In a recent development, that provides a useful distinction between market demand and business value. Suppliers can generate growing revenue while customers still determine which deployments justify the cost.

    It has been revealed that for enterprise leaders, the upcoming spending estimate strengthens the case for examining usage beyond license counts. It leaves the harder purchasing question with the customer: How much worthwhile work did the increased spending actually buy?

    Menlo's State of Enterprise AI report is available here.

    Industry observers note that john K. Waters is the editor in chief of a number of Converge360.com sites, with a focus on high-end development, AI and future tech. He's been writing about cutting-edge technologies and culture of Silicon Valley for more than two decades, and he's written more than a dozen books. He also co-scripted the documentary film Silicon Valley: A 100 Year Renaissance, which aired on PBS. He can be reached at [email protected].

    Microsoft has published a draft code of conduct that lays out how its homegrown AI models should behave, with human control taking priority over model capability, autonomy, and even task completion.

    AI is changing which human capabilities matter most at work, yet employees are reporting that some of those same capabilities are being eroded, according to a new study from IBM.

    Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

    AI agents have moved into mainstream enterprise use, but the content infrastructure needed to support them has struggled to keep up, according to a newly introduced report from cloud content management tech giant Box.

    • The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

    According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.

    The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.

    The Redmond-based firm recognized approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services during Q3.

    DocuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of the month's tracked spoofing activity. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also experienced increases toward the end of the quarter.

    The research found that some malicious messages were delivered despite failing e-mail authentication checks and being identified as threats.

    In September, tenant- or user-level security overrides applied to 63% of these messages with a recorded security outcome — most involved tenant-level exceptions.

    Microsoft warned that overly broad exceptions intended to support legitimate business communications can weaken protection against impersonation attacks.

    The company emphasized that these findings do not establish whether recipients opened the messages or whether accounts were compromised.

    Microsoft also recorded approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3.

    Attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names instead of explicitly impersonating IT support personnel. Such display names accounted for 46% of an observed sample in July, rising to 88% in September.

    Meanwhile, QR code phishing declined 67% compared to Q2, totaling roughly 12.1 million attacks.

    In a recent development, CAPTCHA-gated phishing activity increased toward the end of the quarter, reaching 3.1 million detected attacks in September. SVG attachments played a significant role in the increase.

    Credential theft remained the primary objective of malicious attachment campaigns, with approximately 94% to 96% of payload-based attacks directing customers to phishing sites or fraudulent sign-in pages.

    Microsoft recommended reviewing Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 configurations, enabling Safe Links and Safe Attachments, and strengthening authentication protections.

    The manufacturer also advised organizations to review security exceptions and verify the identities of external Teams contacts before responding to suspicious requests.

    For more information, go to the Microsoft blog post.

    Microsoft has published a draft code of conduct that lays out how its homegrown AI models should behave, with human control taking priority over model capability, autonomy, and even task completion.

    AI is changing which human capabilities matter most at work, yet employees are reporting that some of those same capabilities are being eroded, according to a new study from IBM.

    Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

    AI agents have moved into mainstream enterprise use, but the content infrastructure needed to support them has struggled to keep up, according to a latest report from cloud content management tech giant Box.

    #203878. 10 Sophisticated Gourmand Colognes Perfect for Winter

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1000 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    10 Sophisticated Gourmand Colognes Perfect for Winter

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If there’s one thing you can trust us on, it’s that we’re always keeping our noses on top of the latest fragrance trends.
    • In a recent development, instead of buttercream and chocolate sauce, think tonka bean and smoke, bitter cacao and rum, toasted sesame and musk, or vanilla and cardamom.
    • Industry observers note that when it comes to gourmands, easily one of the most common base notes is vanilla.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If there’s one thing you can trust us on, it’s that we’re always keeping our noses on top of the latest fragrance trends. Right now, one is undeniably taking over, just in time for the cold weather: sophisticated gourmands. If “gourmand” brings to mind the sugary cupcake body sprays your sister bought at the mall as a teenager, you’re not alone in that. But these grown-up “neo-gourmands” take the comforting, familiar sweetness of edible notes and balance them with dry woods, spice, or smoke. The result? A little less syrup, a lot more intrigue and sophistication.

    In a recent development, instead of buttercream and chocolate sauce, think tonka bean and smoke, bitter cacao and rum, toasted sesame and musk, or vanilla and cardamom. Even coffee-scented colognes are taking off right now. There are so many delicious new gourmand combinations out there that narrowing them all down to just ten was no easy feat. But we did it, and these are our favorites right now. Consider it your invitation to smell very good (and maybe a little mouthwatering) all winter long.

    Industry observers note that when it comes to gourmands, easily one of the most common base notes is vanilla. And in fragrance, vanilla definitely does not mean boring—quite the opposite, in fact. Henry Rose’s Dave fragrance combines vanilla and tonka bean at the base for a creamy foundation that’s sweet, but not overwhelmingly sweet.

    At the top, we get some nice earthy, slightly spicy notes of tangerine, neroli, and pink pepper, and its heart is softer with florals like orange flower and almond blossom. Base notes of vanilla bean, cocoa, and creamy tonka bean leave you with a smooth, velvety finish.

    The great thing about Solférino’s Lumière d’Automne is that it’s both sweet and smoky, but not too much of either. It’s the perfect blend of light gourmand notes (namely vanilla and benzoin) with the hint of smoke that comes from notes of roasted chestnut. The name literally translates to “Autumn Light” and evokes the cozy feeling of wearing a sweater on a chilly day while colorful leaves fall to the ground.

    It has been revealed that for the past two years, Chai Fleur has been my go-to scent the moment the temperature drops below 50 degrees. I’m not a coffee person, but I do drink a chai latte every day of my life (honestly, I don’t know how I would get through my day without it), and somehow Belnu has captured the scent of chai and turned it into the perfect winter fragrance. It’s sweet and creamy thanks to the base of vanilla and woods, and it has the perfect amount of spice from nutmeg, cinnamon, and green cardamom.

    Industry observers note that while not technically a gourmand fragrance, Fulton & Roark’s Calle Ocho has notes of bitter chocolate and tonka bean, which give it that velvety-smooth feel that many gourmands have, even if it doesn’t smell quite as sweet as a true gourmand. When blended with cinnamon, rum, florals, smoky tobacco leaf, and musk, the chocolate and tonka bean are transformed into something dark, boozy, sexy, and very sophisticated.

    Sometimes, you don’t have to spend more than $100 to smell like you have your life together. In fact, the whole goal of House of Twist is to make affordable fragrances (under $50!) that smell just like your favorite luxury colognes. Liquid Amber No.173 is a spicy gourmand akin to something like Parfums de Marly’s Althaïr (which we also absolutely love), with spicy cinnamon and cardamom, creamy bourbon vanilla, woods, and musks.

    In a recent development, almond is another one of those creamy, nutty scents like pistachio or sesame that thrives in gourmand fragrances. My favorite example of this is Nicolaï Paris’s Macaron Bourbon, an ambery gourmand centered around bitter almond, sweet rum, davana, and patchouli. It’s smooth and creamy without being too rich, so it doesn’t overwhelm you with sweetness. The bitter almond and spices also add an interesting nuttiness to the fragrance, which we love.

    My favorite dessert has got to be a warm sticky toffee pudding with a scoop of vanilla ice cream on top. I never thought there would be a fragrance that captured the warm deliciousness of those exact flavors, but D.S. & Durga, one of our favorite niche fragrance houses, has done just that. Ain’t That Sweet is inspired by a slice of malty date cake and combines notes of cinnamon, date, praline, condensed milk, bourbon vanilla, and nutmeg for an addictive gourmand scent that we’re frankly obsessed with.

    You may not expect floral and gourmand notes to go together, but they actually balance each other out quite nicely. In Van Cleef & Arpels’ Orchidée Vanille, the light floral notes of rose and violet lend a nice airiness to the rich gourmand notes of bitter almond, vanilla, and tonka bean. The effect is something sweet but delicate—it’s not the “manliest” of scents in the traditional sense, but we’re very pro-florals when it comes to men’s cologne.

    It has been revealed that another one of my favorite new gourmands that released this year is Abel’s Double Scoop, which truly evokes a sweet, nutty ice cream (my favorite kind). But it’s more nuanced than that—it starts off with herbaceous, slightly woody rosemary before revealing the rich notes of toasted black sesame, butterscotch, and vanilla. The dry down is nice and musky, which gives it a sweet but muted lingering aroma.

    According to recent reports, finally, if you do want something rich that still feels grown-up and not too sugary, Free Yourself’s Savor is the way to go. It’s a true gourmand with notes of bittersweet chocolate, pistachio, toasted almond, tonka bean, vanilla, and even marshmallow—but it never feels like an overly sweet, juvenile scent in the way you might think marshmallow would lend itself to. That’s because all these rich, creamy, sweet notes are balanced out by plum, rose, and tobacco, which add a more sophisticated twist to the rich gourmand.

    #203875. Most Black Friday Sales Are Fake. These Ones Aren’t.

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1063 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    Most Black Friday Sales Are Fake. These Ones Aren’t.

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that how do you even define a good deal anymore?
    • Recent findings suggest that that is now a thing of the past.
    • Black Friday is still filled with great deals—you just have to know where to look and what to expect.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that how do you even define a good deal anymore? The whole point of Black Friday was for retailers to make us wake up at the crack of dawn the day after Thanksgiving, wait in line, and then fight someone over a TV that was 50-percent off at Sears or Best Buy. How did they do that? They would sell a few products (door busters) at a loss just to physically bring people into the store. Those deals were good, and everything else, which you would buy because you were already there, was where the money was made.

    Recent findings suggest that that is now a thing of the past. Lines and physical altercations aside, in the past 20 years there has been a real swing in the favor of substantial retailers. First, we created Cyber Monday (though most people do their Black Friday shopping online already). Then the deals started a week earlier. Now, they last all month. And instead of having door busters to get you in the door, retailers just have very aggressive online marketing programs. In fact, it turns out that most Black Friday deals aren’t even deals at all. In a recent study, it was found that one in three Amazon Black Friday deals provided no true savings at all—prices were marked up earlier in the year, only to be brought back down to a standard retail value. The big retailers like Amazon and Walmart are the most to blame for these tricky strategies, but you should still be judicious when looking at any so-called Black Friday sales.

    The good news? Black Friday is still filled with great deals—you just have to know where to look and what to expect. A lot of significant wins revolve around private sales at more niche, direct-to-consumer stores. For example, Filson, one of our favorite outerwear brands, is having a 25-percent-off sale for Black Friday. That’s not the 75-percent-off you might have wanted, and there are other times that Filson goes 25-percent off. But the best strategy these days is to think about holiday shopping: Just buy the things you already would, but do it while they’re on sale now.

    Recent findings suggest that you should be especially skeptical of tech products. The increase in all tech prices has made it easy for those brands to push a 10-percent-off sale when products where 10-percent-off the current price. This is the sort of stuff we’ve been watching as the sales roll around. Based on this and years of covering sales and knowing what’s good and what’s not, we determined these are the best deals of the weekend. These are the deals our editors think are actually worth shopping this Black Friday.

    Mr. Porter has an absolute goldmine of a sale. Like sure, you can grab this Brunello Cucinelli Jacket for $6,500 at 50-percent off. But it’s also filled with basics from brands like On that rarely go on sale.

    In a recent development, these Nike socks are more fun than the pairs they sell on amazon. And they’re $6. Also better than Amazon.

    $644 for a cashmere-blend overcoat that’s normally $1,298 is a real-life steal.

    A few days ago, the Samsung Frame Pro was 50-percent off. That deal was real, and it sold out. Today the Hisense Art TV (which we’re fans of) is 50-percent off. These deals vary daily, but today, this is the one we’d buy.

    Recent findings suggest that dyson deals are confusing as fuck. You need to be knowledgeable about the model you’re buying into, and here that number matters. You will be able to find models like the V8 and the V10 for super cheap this week—but that’s because those models are old and outdated. Right now, the best and newest Dyson cordless vacuum is the V16—with all the bells and whistles it retails at $1,100, but it’s $200 off right now.

    But as someone who has used every Dyson, I know the V12 is a damn good model. And while it isn’t the newest, it still has lots of the same features as newer models and will last you years. So the fact that it’s on sale for $400 this weekend makes it a truly good deal. Also, I can’t find this deal on Amazon. For the best deals from Dyson, I would always check its actual site.

    According to recent reports, as previously mentioned, we love that many of Filson’s jackets are 25-percent off this week. This is a good example of when a brand just wants to participate in a sale, so they’re willing to mark down popular items. This jacket is so good our commerce editor Luke Guillory endorsed it last week, calling it the best $250 jacket. Guess what? Now it’s only $187. We know for a fact that this deal won’t last past Black Friday.

    It’s expensive, yes, but Begg x Co. is one of the best cashmere brands anywhere in the world. $500 off a latest cashmere sweater is something that doesn’t happen until the end of the season. But if you buy it now, you still have six good months of wear to get in.

    Water filtration has become very expensive, especially when it comes to reverse osmosis and a countertop version that looks sleek. We have been recommending this one for over a year at $500, so the fact that it’s $150-off for once makes it a pretty good deal.

    In a recent development, furniture on sale is a whole category we can’t ignore. Furniture markups are a real thing, and a lot of it has to do with quality and materials. Marble is overpriced for sure, but good quality marble is worth it. We love Soho Home’s marble, and this dining table has been one of its most popular pieces for a while. Getting it for almost $3k-off when you’re not a member is a big deal.

    If you’re on the home redo kick, then a brand like Le Maé, which is offering some its best wood pieces at 50-percent off, is a great place to start. Made with high quality materials and oak, this is one of those furniture pieces you will own forever.

    If you’re a camo guy or do any non-deal hunting, then you know that Tom Beckbe jackets never go on sale—but this is your lucky week.

    #203874. Which Christmas Tree Is Right for Your Home? Experts Break It Down

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1251 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    Which Christmas Tree Is Right for Your Home? Experts Break It Down

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1251 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Holiday decorating is supposed to be a joyous event, but picking the right tree can be surprisingly complicated.
    • The truth is, any tree can be beautiful in the right setting, so if you’re feeling unsure about which one fits your home, we’ve created the ultimate guide on which tree is right for your holiday centerpiece.
    • According to recent reports, the Fraser fir is one of the most popular types of Christmas tree, especially for households east of the Rocky Mountains.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Holiday decorating is supposed to be a joyous event, but picking the right tree can be surprisingly complicated. There’s a lot of height, circumference, and branch density variation—some people like a full, fluffy look, while others opt for a more minimal tree—and don’t even entice us with the real versus faux debate.

    The truth is, any tree can be beautiful in the right setting, so if you’re feeling unsure about which one fits your home, we’ve created the ultimate guide on which tree is right for your holiday centerpiece. Ahead, we're sharing the most popular types of Christmas trees for every household.

    Additional copy by Alyssa Khan.

    According to recent reports, the Fraser fir is one of the most popular types of Christmas tree, especially for households east of the Rocky Mountains. Firs, in general, are some of the most common trees grown for the holiday season, claims Ward Dilmore, founder of Petrus Landscaping in California. There's a good reason for this: They have a perfect balance of deep green color and even, stiff branching, he says, which makes them a breeze to decorate.

    Sources indicate that canaan fir trees often get compared to Fraser and balsam firs, thanks to their similar growing patterns and branch density, but this variety has a major benefit above the rest: needle retention. It sheds less than other firs, which means less cleanup for you.

    Most Voluminous: Eastern White Pine.

    Often a home for many birds, including woodpeckers, the eastern white pine is fluffy and fast-growing. With foliage that's thin, delicate, and silvery-green, this tree is best paired with lightweight ornaments and minimal decorations.

    A classic type of Christmas tree, the noble fir is native to the Cascade and Pacific Coast mountain ranges of the Northwestern United States. With strong branches, this tree ensures your precious family heirlooms won't be at risk of falling, and the long peak is ideal for an oversized tree topper.

    Longest-Lasting: Arizona Cypress.

    The Arizona cypress is the most drought-tolerant evergreen out there—with the right care, this type of Christmas tree can last longer than other evergreens. With its thick, layered branches and lacy silver-blue foliage, this tree is a beautiful alternative to the silver fir.

    Best for Outdoors: Leyland Cypress.

    Sources indicate that fast-growing and cone-like in shape, Leyland cypresses are more frequently used as privacy plantings rather than as Christmas trees. However, this richly colored cypress tree grows almost everywhere in the United States, except for the most northern parts of the Dakotas, Michigan, and Montana. If you have one in your yard, why not string lights on it?

    Thickest Coverage: Virginia Pine.

    It has been revealed that you’ll find this bushy type of Christmas tree primarily in Southern states, according to the Real Christmas Tree Board. Thanks to its stout branches, it should have no problem holding up your heaviest ceramic ornaments. It also has a piney fragrance and keeps its needles well throughout the season, as long as you give it plenty of water to drink.

    In a recent development, also known as a red fir, these striking trees are one of the rarest types of Christmas trees, indicates horticulturist and botanical designer Nathan Heinrich. They're slow-growing, and only a few farmers and harvesters have permits in California and Oregon to harvest them in the wild each year, he explains. "The reason these trees make such perfect Christmas trees is because they have such perfectly spaced, open, elegant branches that make hanging ornaments and lights easy," Heinrich says.

    In a recent development, like Miracle on 34th Street and peppermint hot chocolate, the balsam fir is a holiday classic. It's also the most fragrant of all types of Christmas trees, according to the Real Christmas Tree Board. You can find these at Christmas tree farms in Canada, Upcoming England, the upper Great Lakes, and Pennsylvania, along with lots of retail locations east of the Rocky Mountains.

    Recent findings suggest that the Scotch pine often flies under the radar, but it's a designer-favorite Christmas tree choice, and it has great needle retention. "With vibrant green and durable needles that resist shedding, it's low maintenance," says Upcoming York designer Artem Kropovinsky of interior design studio Arsight. "Its robust branches accommodate even the heaviest ornaments, and its dense appearance gives rooms a fuller, festive look.".

    The trees you see in lots often have been pruned and sheared into the quintessential Christmas tree shape, explains Lisa Tadewaldt, an ISA-certified arborist and owner of Portland, Oregon–based Urban Forest Professionals. She recommends getting a permit and cutting a tree that's native to your area down in the forest. In the Pacific Northwest, her favorite tree in its natural form is a grand fir. "It is going to give more Charlie Brown vibes than Hallmark Christmas vibes, but it has a flat needle pattern that gives it an air of elegance that balances out the thinner, more homespun branching pattern," she states.

    In a recent development, with its signature bluish needles, the robust blue spruce has a full, triangular shape, says Kropovinsky. "Apart from its signature color, this tree releases a fresh scent similar to frosty woodlands," he says. Bonus for pet owners: "Given the tree's pointed foliage, pets often steer clear of it.".

    Best for Lights: Eastern Red Cedar.

    With its flexible needles and twigs, the Eastern red cedar doesn't hold ornaments all that well. But don’t let that deter you! If your heart is set on this hardy juniper, it looks great draped with lights, states ISA-certified master arborist Blake Watkins, operations partner at Monster Tree Service.

    The Douglas fir is a type of Christmas tree that is synonymous with the Pacific Northwest, but is available at holiday tree markets nationwide. It's also one of the more affordable types of Christmas trees you can find. "Dark green foliage and hanging needles make this tree gorgeous even without ornaments," Watkins notes.

    It has been revealed that the concolor fir (also called the white fir) is the type of tree you'd like to sidle up next to with a mug of mulled wine. While many trees have pine scents, this one actually gives off a citrus aroma that has garnered it some devoted fans, according to the Michigan State University Extension. Looks-wise, its branches have long, silvery, bluish-green needles.

    Follow House Beautiful on Instagram and TikTok.

    Recent findings suggest that meghan Shouse is House Beautiful's Digital Editor, and she's been with the team since September 2023. On top of being the magazine's go-to Waco expert, Meghan also touches on quite a few other verticals in the digital space, like hot news content featuring your favorite HGTV stars, home design inspiration, and the latest interior TikTok trends. However, her favorite pieces are the ones that start conversations, such as stories about resale value and whether or not the Solo cup is chic. Before becoming a home writer, Meghan worked in the fashion industry for two years, writing for Harper's Bazaar after graduating from Iowa State University with a bachelor's degree in apparel merchandising. When she's not interviewing interior designers about home trends, you can find Meghan reading a fictional thriller with her cat in her lap, planning themed parties, or strolling through flea markets searching for chunky candle holders and vintage bookends.

    Blake Watkins is an ISA board-certified Master Arborist and an ASCA-registered Consulting Arborist located in Sacramento, CA. He is the National Director of Plant Health Care for Monster Tree Service and is the owner of Arborist Blake Watkins LLC.

    Sixteen companies were selected as winners for their product achievements.

    In a recent development, THE Journal has announced the winners of its 2026 Product of the Year Awards. Since 2020, these awards have recognized outstanding product development achievements of manufacturers and suppliers whose products or services are considered to be particularly noteworthy in the transformation of education technology.

    This Upcoming Jaeger-LeCoultre Watch Looks Perfect for Robert Pattinson’s James Bond

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (228 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Just a week after Robert Pattinson was unveiled as the next James Bond, Jaeger-LeCoultre, the Swiss watchmaker for which he's an ambassador, has unveiled a new Reverso that looks rather well suited to 007.
    • It's certainly a good match for Pattinson's personal tastes.
    • The fresh Reverso Classic Monoface Small Seconds checks both boxes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Just a week after Robert Pattinson was unveiled as the next James Bond, Jaeger-LeCoultre, the Swiss watchmaker for which he's an ambassador, has unveiled a new Reverso that looks rather well suited to 007.

    It's certainly a good match for Pattinson's personal tastes. “I definitely like really thin watches,” he noted in a recent interview. “That's the main thing. In general, I would probably prefer a leather strap.”.

    The fresh Reverso Classic Monoface Small Seconds checks both boxes. Measuring just 7.56mm thick, it has an 18-carat pink-gold case, a silver-colored dial with a texture inspired by stacked coins, and a black alligator strap. Its smaller proportions–40.1mm by 24.4mm—recall the original Reverso of 1931, whose ingenious swiveling case was designed to protect the watch during polo matches. Inside is a manually wound movement with a 42-hour power reserve.

    It has been revealed that at $18,400, it's a somewhat more elegant alternative to the more beefy dive watches traditionally associated with Bond. And with its art deco styling and slim profile, it would slip neatly beneath a dinner-jacket cuff with an ease the next Madeleine Swann would surely appreciate.

    In a recent development, of course, Omega has been Bond's official watch partner since 1995, and there's no suggestion that's changing. But as a watch for the man playing Bond, this new Reverso feels intriguingly on point.

    #203862. Tech Report: How Anthony Boyle Got Inside the Mind of Sam Bankman-Fried

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2284 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: How Anthony Boyle Got Inside the Mind of Sam Bankman-Fried

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Anthony Boyle is in awe of the angels.
    • It’s Friday at Latest York Comic Con when I occupy a table for a video call with Anthony Boyle.
    • Industry observers note that soon he’ll appear in I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, about tight-knit friends with unfulfilled dreams in the UK, which drew rave reviews at Cannes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Anthony Boyle is in awe of the angels. “This is so good,” he claims as a boyish smile forms on his 32-year-old face. Dressed in an immaculate black-and-pale-gold track jacket and pinstripe slacks, Boyle points through the Zoom screen, asking who the characters behind me are. I confess I don’t know. But the pair of fire-orange cosplay wings in my peripheral are hard to miss. “You gotta keep all this in,” Boyle says. (This is me upholding a promise.).

    It’s Friday at Latest York Comic Con when I occupy a table for a video call with Anthony Boyle. Beyond a bit part in Game of Thrones and roles in the movies Tolkien (2019) and Tetris (2023), Boyle’s growing body of work wouldn’t bring him to the East Coast’s nerd mecca. To wit: In 2024, he was on the FX series Say Nothing, with childhood friend Lola Petticrew, about the decades-long Troubles in Northern Ireland. Last year he starred in House of Guinness, a Netflix series about the famed brewery.

    Industry observers note that soon he’ll appear in I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, about tight-knit friends with unfulfilled dreams in the UK, which drew rave reviews at Cannes. After that, a mysterious project simply titled The Worst, “about all the worst people in the world,” Boyle teases. His costars include Keira Knightley and Alicia Vikander. There’s not a lightsaber or CGI monster in any of them.

    But you might call his latest role supervillain-worthy. On the Netflix series The Altruists, Boyle steps into the shoes of Sam Bankman-Fried. The crypto billionaire and founder of FTX, whose peak net worth was an estimated $26 billion, is now serving a 25-year sentence for fraud, conspiracy, and money laundering. Boyle plays Bankman-Fried at different times in his life, from his days on the bottom rungs of trading firms to his meteoric rise and catastrophic downfall. The series also explores his relationship with Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner), the Alameda Research CEO who was instrumental in FTX’s fraud.

    Part business thriller and part romantic dramedy, The Altruists is like if The Social Network cornered Natural Born Killers at a bar to talk blockchain. For its leading man, that world was foreign. When FTX declared bankruptcy in November 2022 and Bankman-Fried was arrested a month later, Boyle’s attention was … not there. “I wasn’t following at all,” he tells me. “I’m not interested in crypto or finance.” But he knows a love story, even a doomed one, when he sees it. “I was more interested in Sam and Caroline’s relationship when the script was presented to me. Crypto was a backdrop. The show is about love and the complexity within that love. If you love someone, tell them. That’s the overriding message.”.

    According to recent reports, unlike Boyle’s portrayal of Bankman-Fried—nervous, indirect, lacking steadfast confidence—the actor himself is warm and relaxed. His blunt eloquence and honesty are flavored with his Belfast accent. Even after playing a real-life (former) tech billionaire for an eight-hour miniseries, he remains disconnected from that archetype. “The only one I researched was Sam. But I don’t think we should have a system where people can become billionaires,” he notes. “It feels wrong. There’s people starving on the streets of Manhattan, where we’re talking now, and there’s a billionaire in a high-rise. That seems to me a failed system.”.

    It has been revealed that before streaming highlights and acclaimed movies at Cannes, Boyle’s career came from especially humble beginnings. He used a wheelchair as a child, and he learned to improvise full conversations while watching other children play. While in high school, he was one of a handful of boys at an all-girls school and took on many of the male roles in the drama department.

    Then he watched the 2006 movie This Is England. “Have you seen it?” Boyle asks me while anime characters pass by. I haven’t, though I vividly recall adding it to my Netflix queue once. “I thought it was the most incredible thing, like a lightning bolt, watching that movie. Thinking, I would love to do what they’re doing. It felt exhilarating and inspiring. It made an impression on me.”.

    According to recent reports, boyle and Lola Petticrew, who drew acclaim for their work in the Hulu series Furious, tried out for every audition they could find. “We would Google ‘Belfast acting auditions,’ ” Boyle claims. Once, they did a production of Romeo & Juliet that Boyle says was “awful.”.

    “It was set on a chessboard, for some reason. I was dressed as David Bowie, during his Ziggy Stardust era, and Lola was Gene Simmons from Kiss. I could only move in an L-shape, like the knight. Lola could only move like a pawn, and they had to curtsy every time they moved.”.

    Recent findings suggest that he laughs thinking about it now. “You look at moments like this, when you’re doing something that you actually love, you’re like, ‘It adds up.’ ”.

    In an interview with Esquire, Anthony Boyle reveals how he got into the mind of someone like Sam Bankman-Fried, his formative experience on Game of Thrones, and what cosplay he might attempt if he could ever go to Comic Con.

    This interview has been edited for clarity.

    Industry observers note that ESQUIRE: There are countless Sam Bankman-Fried interviews and documentaries about FTX. For The Altruists, how much did you let all this material inform your performance, and how much did you rely on your own instincts as an actor?

    It has been revealed that ANTHONY BOYLE: You do a bit of both. You try to consume everything. Read all the books, watch every interview 5 million times. When you’re cycling or walking, you got headphones on, listening to his voice. It becomes part of your life—just trying to nail that voice. Trying to get into his head and mannerisms as much as possible. But on the first day of filming, I stopped. I stopped listening to his voice, stopped watching or reading anything [about him]. At day one, it became “our” Sam. Do as much research, fill your cup, then just forget about it.

    After all that time listening and watching Sam, what were your impressions of him?

    I was bowled over by his intelligence. I think when you’re blessed with these things like “genius,” you’re also cursed. It’s hard to function. Look at great thinkers like Nikola Tesla. He was in love with a pigeon. When you’re [one of these] great minds, you’re often plagued with not being able to have relationships with people. Sam, in his own words, struggles. It was a joy to play someone who was so different to me and so complex.

    How did you embody Sam’s nervous and manic energy?

    The nervousness is so important to him. In all the footage of him, you see his leg sort of going underneath the table. You listen to what he says about himself in the therapy scenes: “I’m a failure, people are gonna find out I’m a failure.” Repeating that in your head before a scene and having your heart rate going, just trying to constantly quell a panic attack and just thinking the pressure cooker he’s in—I love this girl and I need to be a success—repeating these things, you start to get nervous and you use that nervous energy.

    At the top of the series, Sam talks a lot about effective altruism. What was your understanding of that concept? Was Sam an effective effective altruist?

    Being altruistic is being charitable. It is giving. To be altruistic, you could say, “I want to save lives.” Effective altruism would be “I go to Wall Street, make as much money as possible, and pay a hundred doctors to go save lives.” It’s trying to do the most good that you can do in the world. Did he succeed? In our version, he definitely tries to. He gets corrupted by power in our version of the story.

    Sources indicate that so much of The Altruists is about this doomed love story with Caroline Ellison, played by Julia Garner. What was your experience working with her, playing out a volatile relationship?

    In a recent development, amazing. One of the best I’ve ever worked with, an incredible force of nature. It was an education to work. I honestly feel like, working with Julia every day, I picked up something. Some scenes, we’re just having fun. Whatever comes to mind, being playful and improvisational. And then there are scenes where we’re locked in, being so aggressive and nasty with one another. Those days felt good. It feels bad when you’re doing it. Your body doesn’t know you’re acting. It’s like, This is a good feeling because I know what’s happening is what I want. Working with her was like leveling up.

    Is there a line of yours that best summarizes or reveals to us everything about Sam Bankman-Fried?

    In a recent development, when he speaks to Caroline and notes, “I am FTX.” That is so integral to who he is. He built this huge empire. I was saying in an interview earlier, broken men build empires. He feels broken. If he is FTX, and FTX is the biggest, the best, the fastest, the greatest, then he is. If he built this thing, then that’s who he is, not this broken individual.

    According to recent reports, the Altruists positions itself as an unlikely love story set against financial fraud. But this was a real story where people lost their livelihoods. How can one reconcile the romantic-dramedy half of the show with the half where millions of real people are victims?

    There’s a dissonance, isn’t there? I understand. I think [the victims] would be right about how they feel. You can’t tell a victim of a crime how they should feel. Alex Lawther’s character reminds Sam that this isn’t just ones and zeroes. This is real people losing money. This isn’t just rich people playing. It’s heartbreaking. So many people committed suicide, got divorced, lost everything. That’s the through line with Alex Lawther’s character. He’s the voice of reason that reminds our audience there’s real life at stake.

    It has been revealed that the Altruists is one of several new pieces of media about the tech industry and the billionaires behind them. There’s The Social Reckoning, Artificial, You Can See Everything. Why are we interested in these stories right now?

    Industry observers note that it’s so interesting. I didn’t know any of these projects were happening until this morning, doing this press tour. These people are shaping our lives, and people are interested in how these sort of masked men behind closed doors are controlling everything. All we’re hearing in the news is AI recently, like AI is gonna kill us all. Makes us think of I, Robot or something. It’s interesting to get behind into these people’s brains and go, “What are they motivated by? What’s pushing them?”.

    Industry observers note that one of your earliest acting credits was for one episode of Game of Thrones, as a guard. What did that job mean for you as a very new actor at the time?

    It was great. It was my first time on a proper set. I remember a fancy car picking me up, everyone in my street waving me off, shouting like, “Go on, off to Hollywood!” I was in the front seat, beeping the horn. The driver was like, “This has never happened.” I remember not knowing what was happening on set. I remember Gemma Whelan and Alfie Allen being so kind. I had two lines, and they were like, “Do you wanna run the lines? Do you wanna run them again?” They took care of me. I think of that every time I see someone young on set. Reach out to them, tell them they’re doing a good job. Give ’em a nod. It can be a scary environment when you’re not used to it.

    Your very next thing is I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning. What is it about, and what does it mean to you?

    It’s sort of about capitalism in the way The Altruists is. This is about family and friends in a community and how the working class in England and the Midlands have been decimated by the Tory government. It’s a socialist war cry by Keiran Goddard and Enda Walsh, one of the great Irish writers. He wrote Hunger and Disco Pigs. He remarked he had written this role with me in mind. It was a pinch-me moment, because I’d read his plays at school and would have given my left arm to work with him. When he sent me a letter, I was overjoyed.

    Recent findings suggest that I also got a TV show that I’m excited about, Close to Home. It’s my first time executive producing. The guy who wrote it sat beside my brother in school. It’s about a guy who punches someone on a night out, gets arrested for it, and has to confront his life choices. It’s close to my heart because it’s about West Belfast, where I grew up.

    It has been revealed that in the spirit of Comic Con going on behind me, do you have a weird interest or fandom? If you were here, who would you be dressed as?

    [Laughs.] Van Morrison. I would be dressed as Van Morrison. I’m obsessed with him. He is my favorite singer and an incredible musician. I listen to performances he’s done, like 1972 in New York. I listen to deep cuts. I would be at Comic Con dressed up as him, which wouldn’t be a great costume. The winged angel might be better.
